title: launch density phase decomposition experiment 2026-01
content:
Purpose / TL;DR:
We ran a focused experiment to decompose GPU-side occupancy and utilization by temporal phase, with the goal of understanding how kernel launch density (inter-launch gaps) correlates with SM saturation and tail latency. Hypothesis: periods with high density of short kernel launches produce lower sustained tensor-core utilization than fewer, longer kernels (because of launch overheads, SM divergence, and scheduling jitter). Also looking for interactions with KV cache activity and CUDA Graph warmup patterns.

Background / why this matters:
- Recent production tail spikes are correlated with short, bursty inference requests (micro-batching disabled) where the runtime emits many small kernels (attention + rotary + layernorm) in quick succession.
- Prior traces show underutilized tensor cores during these bursts even when aggregate occupancy appears reasonable in sampling tools. We want to move beyond static occupancy numbers to time-resolved phase-level analysis.

Experiment setup:
- Model/Workload: distilled-16k-transformer-infer (production-like config), sequence length 1024 sample, batch size 1/2/4 sweep.
- Hardware: p4d (A100) node, CUDA 12.4, driver 535.86, cuDNN 9.1.
- Runtime build: serving-runtime@bench/launch-density-sweep (PR 542 experimental knobs: microbatcher disabled, compile flags: -DUSE_ASYNC_COPY=1 -DLAUNCH_AGGREGATION=0).
- Profilers: NVIDIA Nsight Systems (nsys) for timeline traces, Nsight Compute (ncu) for per-kernel metrics, nvtx annotations from runtime to mark phases.
- Capture commands used:
  - nsys profile --trace=nvtx,cuda --output=nsys/ld_phase_run1 --sample=none ./bench_infer --seq 1024 --batch 1
  - ncu --target-processes all --metrics sm_efficiency,achieved_occupancy,ipc,warp_execution_efficiency ./bench_infer --seq 1024 --batch 1
  - small python runner that emits microsecond timestamps around host launch points for correlation with nsys export.

Data collection notes:
- Each run captured 2000 tokens of generation. We recorded cold-first-token runs and steady-state runs (after 20 tokens) to separate graph-warmup artifacts.
- For CUDA Graph experiments, we compared three modes: cold (no graph), graph-warm (first run constructs graph), graph-replay (replay-only).
- Added an nvtx range around KV cache hits/evictions to see if hostcopy or hash lookups align with gaps.

Analysis approach (phase decomposition):
1) Convert nsys timeline to CSV with per-kernel start/end timestamps.
2) Compute inter-launch gap = start_time(next) - end_time(current) for consecutive kernels.
3) Cluster timeline into phases by gap density: dense-phase (median gap < 40us), sparse-phase (median gap > 200us), and transition-phase. Thresholds chosen based on histogram elbow.
4) For each phase, aggregate kernel types (matmul, softmax, layernorm, fused-elemwise), occupancy, achieved_tflops proxy, and host-to-device memcpy coverage.
5) Visualize a heatmap (time on x, SM utilization on y) and a launch-density plot (bars show kernel counts per 1ms window).

Key findings (summary):
- Dense-phase inefficiency: Dense phases with many short kernels (avg duration 8-15us) showed markedly lower tensor-core activity despite high SM occupancy reported by ncu. Achieved TFLOP proxy and IPC fall by ~25% relative to long-kernel phases.
- Inter-launch stalls: A non-trivial fraction (~12%) of dense-phase time is consumed by scheduling overheads (gaps 5-30us) that are not host memcpy; they line up with small kernel submission overheads seen in host trace.
- CUDA Graph effect: When using CUDA Graph replay, kernel inter-launch gaps collapse to near-zero and many short kernels fuse into a single graph node. This restores TFLOP utilization to expected levels and reduces end-to-end latency by ~18% for batch=1 steady-state. However, graph construction/varianting is brittle: sequence-length dependent code paths caused graph misses in ~7% of traces (we saw fallback to non-graph path).
- KV cache interaction: Periods labeled with KV-eviction NVTX correlate with small host copies and a spike in inter-launch gaps immediately after eviction. Eviction + hostcopy introduces a 150-400us window where the next compute kernel is delayed, causing a visible utilization trough.
- Batch size sensitivity: Increasing batch to 4 reduces launch density (more work per kernel) and smooths utilization; however, customer constraints often require batch 1.

Representative trace snippets (observations):
- Example run, batch=1, steady-state: sequence of kernels: matmul(12us), fused-attn(9us), elemwise(7us), layernorm(6us), softmax(10us) with gaps of 20-35us between many of them. ncu reports achieved_occupancy ~0.65 for matmul but IPC/warp_efficiency low.
- With graph replay: single large kernel node (combined) duration ~80us; no pauses observed; tensor-core efficiency up ~30%.

Open questions / anomalies:
- Why does ncu achieved_occupancy diverge from effective TFLOP output in dense phases? Suspect per-warp divergence and memory bandwidth underutilization due to small gemm shapes. Need microbenchmarks to isolate tensor-core utilization for small M/N/K shapes.
- Are some of the short kernels hitting mixed-precision paths that trigger slow fallback code? We saw a handful of kernels with instruction mix indicative of scalar operations.
- Graph misses: need to catalogue all code paths that lead to graph invalidation (positional embedding length, rotary fused vs unfused, attention mask shapes).

Next steps / action items:
- (Marco) Produce microbench: param sweep of GEMM shapes matching our fused-attn inner dims to measure small-kernel tensor-core efficiency. Target date: 2026-01-20.
- (Lina) Instrument runtime to add a "kernel aggregation" mode where we attempt to merge back-to-back kernels on the host-side (software coalescing) and measure effect without full CUDA Graph. Target: 2026-01-22.
- (Aisha) Bulk run graph replay stability tests across seq lengths 32/128/512/1024 to produce miss rate heatmap and attach to PR 542. Target: 2026-01-18.
- Add unit tests that assert no KV-eviction-hostcopy occurs during steady-state inference for critical low-latency routes; if eviction unavoidable, schedule it during warm periods.

Notes to self / miscellaneous observations:
- nsys export to chrome trace + my python parser worked better than the built-in timeline viewer for computing exact inter-launch gaps (viewer rounds timestamps).
- Use ncu --kernel-id-only to quickly map out hot kernels; then run per-kernel ncu slices for deeper metrics.
- Consider enabling persistent kernel strategy for very short kernels (persistent SM loops) but that requires refactor of fused ops to be long-running.

References and links:
- internal linear task: RUN-213 (launch-density sweep)
- runtime PR: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/542
- slack thread: #serving-runtime 2026-01-13 (high level traces)

Conclusion:
The phase-decomposition view is useful: it explains why static occupancy numbers can be misleading. Launch density is a first-class performance dimension for inference workloads, especially at batch=1. Immediate mitigation with CUDA Graph replay looks promising but is not a silver bullet due to graph miss conditions. Short-term engineering work should focus on graph coverage and host-side aggregation, medium-term work on kernel fusion/persistent-kernel patterns and microkernel tuning.

Attachments (local):
- nsys traces saved under s3://redwood-telemetry/ld_phase/ (run1..run6)
- ncu csv exports under s3://redwood-telemetry/ld_ncu_exports/
